lines.text: אבי 6 אבי
אֲבִיהוּא (to whom He, i. e. God, is
father) pr. n. Abihu, a son of Aaron,
slain by fire from God for offering un-
lawful sacrifice, Lev. 10, 1 sq.
אֲבִיהוּד (whose father is Judah, i. q.
אֲבִי יְהוּדָה) Abihud, pr. n. m. 1 Chr. 8, 3.
אֲבִיהַיִל (perh. for אֲבִיחַיִל) Abihail,
pr. n. f. a) The wife of Rehoboam, 2
אֶבְיוֹן adj. (r. אָבָה no. 2) 1. needy,
poor, Deut. 15, 4. 7. 11. Sons of the
needy, i. e. the needy, the poor, Ps. 72,
4; see בֵּן no. 8.
2. poor, i. e. afflicted, distressed,
wretched, often coupled with synon. עָנִי.
Ps. 40, 18 וַאֲנִי עָנִי וְאֶבְיוֹן and I am poor
and afflicted. 70, 6. 81, 1. 109, 22.—Spec.
like עָנִי, spoken of one who suffers un-
justly, with the accessory idea of humble
and pious feeling; whence in Am. 2, 6
צַדִּיק and אֶבְיוֹן are joined. Also of a
whole people subjected to suffering and
calamity, e. g. the Israelites in exile, Is.
41, 17; comp. 25, 4. In the same sense
the sect of the Ebionites adopted this
name, as being οἱ πτωχοὶ τῷ πνεύματι, ὧν
ἐστιν ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν Matt. 5, 3.
אֲבִיּוֹנָה f. pr. desire, appetite, lust, from
r. אָבָה no. 1; then the caper-berry, which
is said to be a provocative of appetite and
lust, Plut. Quæst. Symp. 6. 2. Plin. H.
So Sept. Vulg. Syr. The Rabbins use
the plur. אֲבִיּוֹנִין not only for caper-ber-
ries, but also for the small fruits or berries
of other trees, as the myrtle, olive, etc.
אֲבִיחַיִל (father of might, i. q. mighty)
Abihail, pr. n. m. a) Num. 3, 35. b)
1 Chr. 5, 14. c) The father of Esther,
אֲבִיטוּב (father of goodness) Abitub,
pr. n. m. 1 Chr. 8, 21.
אֲבִיטַל (whose father is the dew) Abi-
tal, pr. n. of one of David’s wives, 2 Sam.
אֲבִיָּם see אֲבִיָּהוּ.
אֲבִימָאֵל m. Gen. 10, 28. 1 Chr. 1, 22,
Abimael, pr. n. of one of the descendants
of Joktan in Arabia, prob. the father or
founder of an Arabian tribe called מָאֵל,
a trace of which Bochart (Phaleg 2. 24)
finds in Theophrast. Hist. Plant. 9. 4;
where the name Μάλι prob. refers to
the same wandering tribe in the vicinity
of the modern Mecca, which Strabo calls
Μειναῖοι, Minæi.
אֲבִימֶ֫לֶךְ (father of the king, or father
king) in pause אֲבִימָ֫לֶךְ, Abimelech, pr. n.
a) Of several kings in the land of the Phi-
listines at different periods of time, Gen.
same king who in Ps. l. c. is called Abi-
melech, in 1 Sam. 21, 11 bears the name
of אָכִישׁ Achish; and hence the former
might seem to be a common title of these
kings, like the پاد شاه Padishah (Pater
Rex) of the Persian kings, and اتاليق
Atâlîk (father, pr. paternity) of the
Khans of Bucharia. b) A son of Gideon,
c) 1 Chr. 18, 16, where the true reading
is prob. אֲחִימֶלֶךְ, as in 2 Sam. 8, 17.
אֲבִינָדָב (father of nobleness, or noble
father) Abinadab, pr. n. m. a) A son
of Jesse, 1 Sam. 16, 8. 17, 13. b) A son
of Saul, 1 Sam. 31, 2. c) 1 Sam. 7, 1.
אֲבִינֹעַם (father of pleasantness or
grace) Abinoam, pr. n. of the father of
Barak, Judg. 4, 6. 5, 1.
אֲבִינֵר (father of a light) Abiner, pr.
n. m. 1 Sam. 14, 50. Elsewhere אַבְנֵר
Abner, q. v.
אֲבִיעֶזֶר (father of help, like Germ.
Adolf, from Atta father and Holf help)
Abiezer, pr. n. m. a) A son of Gilead,
Josh. 17, 2; also meton. of his descend-
ants, Judg. 6, 34. 8, 2. Patronym. is
אֲבִי הָעֶזְרִי the Abi-ezrite Judg. 6, 11. 24.
8, 32.—An abridged form is אִיעֶזֶר Iezer,
Num. 26, 30; and the patronym. אִיעֶזְרִי
ib. b) One of David’s warriors, 2 Sam.
אָבִיר m. subst. (r. אָבַר) one strong,
mighty, only in the formula אֲבִיר יַעֲקֹב,
אֲבִיר יִשְׂרָאֵל, the mighty One of Jacob, of
Israel, spoken of God, Gen. 49, 24. Is. 1, 24.
אַבִּיר adj. (r. אָבַר) 1. strong, mighty,
spoken of persons, and often as subst.
one strong, a mighty one, Judg. 5,
אַבִּירֵי לֵב the strong of heart, stout-
hearted.—Poetically κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν put: a)

line_status.note: Running header: the catchwords are printed unpointed (no hataf-patah or hiriq), so Reading A's vowel points are not on the page; Reading B is exact.

Under the aleph the print shows a compound mark (two stacked dots plus a short stroke), i.e. hataf-patah, not a plain patah; the bet carries a single dot (hiriq), not a shva. Yod has dagesh, vav has holem, nun hiriq, then yod and final nun — matching Reading A.
A short diagonal accent stroke is printed above the מ (between מ and ל) in the headword, marking penultimate stress; Reading B omits it.

A small accent stroke is printed above the mem of the pausal form (marking the penultimate tone, as also on the headword in line 2); Reading B omits it. All other letters and points agree: qamets under mem, segol under lamed, final kaf with sheva, no plene vav.

The elision mark after κατ is printed as a raised curved Greek koronis-style apostrophe in the Greek font, matching Reading A's U+1FBD rather than Reading B's plain ASCII apostrophe; all other characters (ἐξοχήν with acute on η, colon, "a)") are identical in both readings and match the print.
